note: A seed, not a canon. Everything here is a title, year and director I can state with confidence; where I was not sure of a cinematographer or a credit I left the field out rather than guess at it. Add, cut and argue with it — the page reads this file and nothing else.

lanes.craft: Watch it for how it looks and how that was done.
lanes.psych: The lineage this place lives in: lysergic cinema, visual music, experimental animation.
lanes.process: About making things. Useful rather than merely inspiring.

items.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
items.why: The Star Gate is slit-scan — a long exposure dragged past artwork on a motion rig. Douglas Trumbull built the machine. Every tunnel shader since is chasing this.

items.title: Enter the Void
items.why: First-person for two hours, with the camera passing through ceilings. The DMT sequences are the most committed attempt anyone has made at rendering the inside of a trip.

items.title: Altered States
items.why: Hallucination built optically, pre-digital: slides, gels, rear projection. The seams are visible and it works anyway.

items.title: Fantastic Planet
items.why: Cutout animation by Roland Topor. Alien by design rather than by rendering — the movement is stiff on purpose and it makes the world wrong in a way CGI cannot.

items.title: Koyaanisqatsi
items.why: Time-lapse as argument. Also the clearest lesson available in cutting picture to music rather than under it.

items.title: Baraka
items.why: Shot on 70mm with a motion-control rig Fricke built himself. Watch for how long he holds a frame.

items.title: Samsara
items.why: The same method twenty years on, in a world that had gone digital around him.

items.title: The Holy Mountain
items.why: Composed in flat symmetrical tableaux like tarot cards. Steal the staging, not the symbolism.

items.title: El Topo
items.why: The film that invented the midnight movie circuit, which is to say the audience you are probably playing to.

items.title: Eraserhead
items.why: Five years of shooting, and the sound is half the picture. Lynch built the drone before he shot most of it.

items.title: Suspiria
items.why: One of the last films printed by the Technicolor dye-transfer process. Colour as structure rather than decoration — hard primaries, no motivation, no apology.

items.title: Hausu
items.why: Every trick in the optical printer at once, from a director who came out of television commercials. Joyful and completely unhinged.

items.title: Possession
items.why: Watch the camera and the actors negotiate the same space. The blocking is choreography.

items.title: Videodrome
items.why: Rick Baker's effects, and the first film to be properly suspicious of a screen. Ages better every year.

items.title: Naked Lunch
items.why: Chris Walas creatures operated on set. Nothing here is a render and it shows.

items.title: Liquid Sky
items.why: New York no-wave, UV makeup and a cheap colour palette used ruthlessly. A film to raid for a look on no money.

items.title: Blade Runner
items.why: Smoke, backlight and practical neon. Almost every frame has a light source inside it.

items.title: Blade Runner 2049
items.why: The Las Vegas sequence is one colour. Deakins on how far a single hue will carry a scene.

items.title: Barry Lyndon
items.why: Candlelit interiors shot on Zeiss f/0.7 glass built for NASA. The constraint is the style.

items.title: Days of Heaven
items.why: Shot almost entirely in the twenty minutes after sunset. A whole film made of a scheduling decision.

items.title: The Conformist
items.why: Storaro's colour theory, fully formed. Light and shadow carry the politics.

items.title: Apocalypse Now
items.why: Watch it next to Hearts of Darkness and you get the film and its cost in one sitting.

items.title: The Red Shoes
items.why: The ballet sequence is seventeen minutes of in-camera effects. Cardiff was painting with three-strip Technicolor.

items.title: Black Narcissus
items.why: The Himalayas, built at Pinewood. Glass shots and painted backdrops doing what a location could not.

items.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari
items.why: The shadows are painted on the set. The origin point for every stylised unreality since.

items.title: Metropolis
items.why: The Schüfftan process — mirrors marrying actors to miniatures in camera. Still the cheapest way to fake scale.

items.title: Sunrise
items.why: Forced-perspective sets and a camera that moves like it has somewhere to be, in 1927.

items.title: Vampyr
items.why: Shot through gauze to fog the image. Atmosphere achieved by deliberately degrading the picture.

items.title: Stalker
items.why: The shift from sepia to colour, and shots held far past comfort. A lesson in duration.

items.title: Solaris
items.why: Science fiction made of weather and water rather than hardware.

items.title: The Colour of Pomegranates
items.why: A locked camera and figures arranged like an illuminated manuscript. Almost no camera movement in the whole film.

items.title: Daisies
items.why: Colour filters swapped mid-scene, collage, jump cuts. Czech New Wave at its most destructive.

items.title: Valerie and Her Week of Wonders
items.why: Dream logic with no waking frame to return to.

items.title: Alice
items.why: Stop motion with real taxidermy and real objects. Švankmajer makes texture do the frightening.

items.title: Street of Crocodiles
items.why: Twenty minutes, and the single best argument for shallow focus in stop motion.

items.title: Un Chien Andalou
items.why: Cut together to defeat interpretation. Still the reference for images that refuse to resolve.

items.title: Meshes of the Afternoon
items.why: Fourteen minutes that invented most of what people mean by dream sequence.

items.title: Dog Star Man
items.why: Layer upon layer of superimposition, painted and scratched directly on the film.

items.title: Mothlight
items.why: Made with no camera at all — moth wings and leaves pressed between splicing tape and run through an optical printer.

items.title: Lapis
items.why: Dot matrices animated on a converted anti-aircraft gun sight. The direct ancestor of every particle system.

items.title: Arabesque
items.why: Whitney's harmonic motion worked out in code. Read his book Digital Harmony next to it.

items.title: An Optical Poem
items.why: Paper shapes on wires, shot frame by frame to Liszt. Visual music before the phrase existed.

items.title: Motion Painting No. 1
items.why: Painted in oil on perspex, one frame per brushstroke, over nine months.

items.title: Begone Dull Care
items.why: Painted and scratched straight onto the filmstrip, cut to Oscar Peterson. The purest audio-reactive piece ever made, and it is hand-made.

items.title: Neighbours
items.why: Pixilation — stop motion with living people as the puppets.

items.title: A Colour Box
items.why: Painted directly on 35mm and released as a GPO advert. Abstract animation smuggled into a cinema programme.

items.title: Free Radicals
items.why: Scratched into black leader with a needle. White marks on black, and nothing else.

items.title: Rhythmus 21
items.why: Rectangles moving in time. One of the first abstract films there was.

items.title: Ballet Mécanique
items.why: Loops and machine rhythm, decades before anyone had a sampler.

items.title: La Jetée
items.why: Almost entirely still photographs. The one moving shot lands because of everything around it.

items.title: Sans Soleil
items.why: The video-synthesiser passages — Marker calls the machine the Zone — are an artist thinking about image processing out loud.

items.title: Powers of Ten
items.why: Nine minutes, one continuous idea. The best information design ever put on film.

items.title: Akira
items.why: Hand-painted light effects, and animated at a frame rate nobody could afford before or since.

items.title: Ghost in the Shell
items.why: Cel animation composited with early digital. The long wordless city sequence is the whole film's thesis.

items.title: Angel's Egg
items.why: Amano's designs, almost no dialogue, and the patience to let a shot sit.

items.title: Perfect Blue
items.why: Kon's match cuts between realities. The editing is the special effect.

items.title: Paprika
items.why: The parade sequence. Everything Inception did, four years earlier and better.

items.title: Belladonna of Sadness
items.why: Mostly still watercolours panned across by the camera. A budget problem turned into a style.

items.title: Mind Game
items.why: Changes technique every few minutes and never loses the thread.

items.title: Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse
items.by: Bob Persichetti, Peter Ramsey, Rodney Rothman
items.why: Deliberate frame-rate changes, halftone dots and chromatic offset used as a language rather than an effect.

items.title: Loving Vincent
items.why: Every frame oil-painted by hand. Worth it for the making-of alone.

items.title: Waltz with Bashir
items.why: An animated documentary, which should not work and does.

items.title: The Cell
items.why: Eiko Ishioka's costumes and a director from commercials. Shallow and gorgeous, which is sometimes the assignment.

items.title: The Fountain
items.why: The nebulae are macro photography of chemicals in a dish, shot by Peter Parks. They have not dated because they were never renders.

items.title: Under the Skin
items.why: The black void is a real set with a liquid surface, not a composite. Half the film was shot with hidden cameras.

items.title: Mandy
items.why: Reds and blues pushed to the point of damage, with long cross-dissolves. A VJ set that became a film.

items.title: Beyond the Black Rainbow
items.why: Built out of a memory of eighties video sleeves. Glacial, and the grain is the point.

items.title: Climax
items.why: Long takes through a crowd that never lets you stand still.

items.title: The Neon Demon
items.why: Refn is colourblind to mid-tones, which is reportedly why his palettes are this saturated.

items.title: Only God Forgives
items.why: Smith lit Barry Lyndon's gaffer crew into a neon Bangkok. Almost every light is in shot.

items.title: In the Mood for Love
items.why: Shot through doorways and past obstructions, and step-printed to slow the bodies without slowing the sound.

items.title: Chungking Express
items.why: Step-printing and smeared handheld, invented largely because they were shooting fast and cheap.

items.title: Hero
items.why: The same story told four times, each in its own colour. Colour as chapter marker.

items.title: Mad Max: Fury Road
items.why: The action is centre-framed so your eye never hunts. Edited to be legible at speed, which almost nothing else is.

items.title: Children of Men
items.why: The long takes are stitched from several, and knowing that makes them more interesting rather than less.

items.title: The Tree of Life
items.why: Douglas Trumbull again, out of retirement, making the cosmos with chemicals and fluid instead of CGI.

items.title: Arrival
items.why: Young underexposes further than anyone else working. The murk is a choice.

items.title: Moonlight
items.why: Three acts, three film stocks emulated, three palettes for the same person.

items.title: The Grand Budapest Hotel
items.why: Three aspect ratios for three time periods, and miniatures used openly rather than hidden.

items.title: Playtime
items.why: Everything in focus and the joke anywhere in frame. Tati built a city and went bankrupt doing it.

items.title: Speed Racer
items.why: Flat planes of saturated colour and layered wipes. Hated on release, raided constantly since.

items.title: Annihilation
items.why: The Shimmer refracts rather than glows, which is a far stranger and better choice.

items.title: Tetsuo: The Iron Man
items.why: Black and white 16mm, pixilation, and a budget of nothing. Proof that relentless is a style.

items.title: Begotten
items.why: Each frame rephotographed by hand to destroy the greys. A year of work to make an image barely legible.

items.title: A Field in England
items.why: The kaleidoscope passage, in black and white, on a tiny budget.

items.title: Twin Peaks: The Return
items.why: Part 8 is an hour of abstract film in the middle of network television. It should not exist.

items.title: Legion
items.why: Period signifiers deliberately scrambled so no decade holds. Rare television that is composed.

items.title: Hannibal
items.why: Network TV that looks like still life painting. The hallucination transitions are worth stealing wholesale.

items.title: Maniac
items.why: An alternate-eighties built entirely on soundstages.

items.title: Severance
items.why: The floor is the character. Production design doing the work dialogue usually does.

items.title: Scavengers Reign
items.why: An alien ecology that behaves consistently, drawn with enormous restraint.

items.title: The Midnight Gospel
items.why: Animation set against unrelated recorded conversation. The mismatch is the form.

items.title: Devilman Crybaby
items.why: Yuasa with a deadline. Watch how little he draws and how much moves.

items.title: Love, Death & Robots
items.why: An anthology of rendering techniques more than of stories. Useful as a catalogue.

items.title: Jodorowsky's Dune
items.why: The best film ever made about a film that was never made, and about assembling people.

items.title: Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker's Apocalypse
items.why: What it costs when a production goes past the point of control.

items.title: Burden of Dreams
items.why: Herzog dragging a steamship over a hill, and Les Blank watching him mean it.

items.title: Lost in La Mancha
items.why: A production falling apart in real time. More instructive than any success.

items.title: Visions of Light
items.why: Cinematographers explaining their own work, with the footage to hand. The single best primer there is.

items.title: Side by Side
items.why: The film-to-digital argument captured while it was still an argument.

items.title: Rivers and Tides
items.why: Goldsworthy's work collapses repeatedly on camera and he starts again. Watch it for that, not the finished pieces.

items.title: Marina Abramović: The Artist Is Present
items.why: On preparing for work whose medium is your own attention.

items.title: Exit Through the Gift Shop
items.why: Whether or not it is true is the point it is making.

items.title: Cave of Forgotten Dreams
items.why: The oldest art we have, and Herzog noticing the animals were drawn to move in firelight.

items.title: Helvetica
items.why: A whole film about one typeface that is really about why anyone chooses anything.

items.title: Objectified
items.why: Designers on the objects nobody looks at.

items.title: Rams
items.why: Less, but better — from the man who meant it, late in life.

items.title: Abstract: The Art of Design
items.why: One designer per episode, with enough room to actually show the work.

items.title: The Story of Film: An Odyssey
items.why: Fifteen hours, and it keeps leaving Hollywood, which is why it is worth the time.

items.title: Everything Is a Remix
items.why: Copy, transform, combine. The most useful thing anyone has said about influence.

items.title: Sisters with Transistors
items.why: The women who built electronic music, with the tape machines they built it on.

items.title: Sound City
items.why: A room, a desk, and an argument about what a space contributes to a record.
